snippet.title: Orbital Days
snippet.description:
What do astronauts actually do all day? How do they sleep, eat, stay warm and survive the most dangerous moments of a mission?

Orbital Days takes you inside real life in space, one question at a time. Every video answers a single, surprising question about astronauts and life aboard the space station, using real footage and documented facts. No hype, just what life in orbit is really like.

New videos every week. Subscribe and come along for the ride.

channel_configs.cultural_localization: The audience is English-speaking, mostly American. EVERYTHING on screen and in the voice is in English. NUMBERS: US format (1,500,000; 2.5). TEMPERATURES: Fahrenheit first (minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit), on screen always in °F (-250°F, +250°F); add Celsius in the voice only when useful. DISTANCES: miles and feet first (250 miles above Earth), kilometers only as an extra. SPEED: miles per hour (17,500 mph). DATES: US format (November 2, 2000). COMPARISONS: references an American viewer knows (a football field, a school bus, the Empire State Building), computed only from documented numbers. FORBIDDEN: invented facts, records not documented, superlatives without a number, any non-English word on screen. SOURCES: only documented facts (NASA, ESA, astronauts' own accounts); when something is uncertain say so.

snippet.title: Why Astronauts Fear Re-Entry More Than Anything Else
snippet.description:
Why do astronauts fear re-entry more than anything else? In this Orbital Days documentary, we ride a spacecraft from 250 miles above Earth at 17,500 mph down through a wall of plasma that reaches about 3,000°F.

We look at the heat shield, the communications blackout, the narrow re-entry corridor, the Columbia accident on February 1, 2003, and the Apollo 13 return on April 17, 1970. Every fact comes from NASA records and documented astronaut accounts.

If you love space station life, NASA history, and real spaceflight science, subscribe to Orbital Days for more stories from orbit.

snippet.title: Why Aren't Astronauts Afraid to Sleep in Space?
snippet.description:
Why aren't astronauts afraid to sleep in space? On the International Space Station, the sun rises and sets about sixteen times a day, the crew sleeps in bags tied to the wall, and the station moves at 17,500 mph, 250 miles above Earth. This Orbital Days documentary explains how astronauts sleep in orbit, what their cabins look like, how training, alarms and Mission Control keep them safe, and why sleep in space feels so different from sleep at home.

We walk through a real night on the ISS: the sleeping bag, the fans, the light, the noise, the cosmic ray flashes some crews report, and how the station's schedule fools the body clock. We also compare it with Apollo and Skylab nights and with your own bedroom.

All facts come from NASA, ESA and astronauts' own accounts. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more questions about life in space.

snippet.title: How Do Astronauts Survive the Cold of Space Without Heaters?
snippet.description:
How do astronauts survive the freezing cold of space without heaters? The real answer is stranger than you think. Space is not cold like a freezer, and the biggest danger on the International Space Station is often too much heat, not too little.

In this documentary, we put you inside the station at 6 AM and follow the heat. You will learn how radiators, ammonia loops, cooling garments, and shiny insulation keep astronauts comfortable, why a spacewalk swings between -250°F and +250°F, and what really happened to the Apollo 13 crew when the power went out.

Every fact comes from documented NASA and ESA sources and astronauts' own accounts. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more real stories from life in space.

snippet.title: What Do Astronauts Actually Do All Day?
snippet.description:
What do astronauts actually do all day? Step inside the International Space Station and follow a real day in orbit: waking up in a sleeping bag, eating from pouches, exercising two hours to protect your bones, doing science, fixing equipment, and floating out on a spacewalk at +250°F and -250°F.

Learn how the station travels at 17,500 mph about 250 miles above Earth, why astronauts see 16 sunrises every day, how the water recycling system recovers about 98 percent of the water on board, and what the return to Earth really feels like.

All facts come from NASA, ESA, and astronauts' own accounts, and all footage is real NASA archive video. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more daily life in space.
